prompt.context: Your client, Metal Co, is a global company involved in manufacturing parts made from metals, plastics and glass. They have an expertise in a stamping process whereby they use heavy machines to stamp and cut parts from sheets of those raw materials. All their parts are usually made to order. Some examples of those parts include car doors, window panes, dashboards of cars etc. They are headquartered in the US but operate in 200 countries. Like most of the economy, they experienced a severe downturn in 2009. However, they have been able to recover well from a revenue standpoint and year on year revenues have stabilized. But, their profitability is much lower compared to competition and this has put severe pressure on the CEO.
prompt.question: The CEO thinks that there are concerns with the cost structure of the company and wants you to specifically analyze their cost structure.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a profitability target or savings target?
clarifying_info.a: There is no target; the greater the savings the better.
We don't have the numbers but we know that they are stable (low growth).

clarifying_info.q: What activities does Metal Co perform?
clarifying_info.a: Design of parts and manufacturing. They have plants in all the countries since they are involved in heavy and volumetric parts. Sometimes they outsource a part of their activities to smaller companies.
Auto makers, construction companies, electronics companies.

exhibits.title: Total Costs for Metal Co
exhibits.shows: A table of Metal Co's total costs by material category over three years

exhibits.title: Steel Prices for Metal Co
exhibits.shows: A table comparing Metal Co's average local steel costs vs average costs for steel from China, broken down by steel grade, with share of total costs

columns: Avg Local Costs for Metal Co (per ton)
Avg Costs for Steel from China (per ton)

framework: Identify this as a cost structure / profitability problem — focus on cost side, not revenue

Break costs into major buckets: Raw Materials (steel, plastic, glass, aluminum), Labour (plant workers, designers, engineers), Utilities (electricity, water, gas), PP&E / Depreciation of machines, Sales & Marketing (including lobbying), Transportation (inbound raw materials and outbound finished goods), Outsourcing costs (manufacturing and design)
Benchmark each cost category against competition
Prioritize highest-absolute and fastest-growing cost lines (raw materials, especially steel)
Consider whether outsourcing high-margin activities (design) vs. low-margin activities (manufacturing) is affecting overall margins
Assess whether cost increases are driven by volume growth or price per unit

questions.prompt: Question 1: List the cost components you would analyze and explain how you would approach each.
questions.guidance: A strong answer names all seven major buckets: raw materials (steel, plastic, glass, aluminum, others), labour, utilities, PP&E/depreciation, sales & marketing, transportation, and outsourcing costs. The candidate should note that outsourcing high-margin activities like design depresses margins, while outsourcing low-margin activities like manufacturing improves them. They should propose benchmarking costs against competitors and prioritize raw materials, labour, and utilities as the highest-impact items.

questions.prompt: Question 2a: Review Exhibit 1 and share your thoughts and next steps.
questions.guidance: A strong candidate observes: (1) Steel & Plastic costs increased ~50% over two years — anomalous for commodity inputs. (2) Heating/AC and electrical costs (in 'Others' or related) rose then fell, suggesting either cost control or a shift in project mix toward less energy-intensive work (e.g., more infrastructure projects). (3) The candidate should ask whether revenues grew in line with costs — they did not grow at such a high rate, confirming a margin compression. (4) Next step: drill into steel because it has the largest absolute jump ($200M increase over two years) and is the biggest cost line.

questions.prompt: Question 2b: Metal Co anticipates steel consumption will increase 20% by volume next year. Using Exhibit 2, calculate how much they will save by procuring all steel from China instead of locally.
questions.guidance: Key insight: share of costs is in dollar terms; the 20% increase is in volume (tons). Derive last year's volumes from last year's dollar costs and local prices, then apply the 20% volume uplift, then multiply savings per ton. Note: China costs already include transportation and customs duties.

math.setup: Last year total steel costs = $600M. High grade = 60% × $600M = $360M; Low grade = 40% × $600M = $240M. Volume last year: High grade = $360M ÷ $1500/ton = 240K tons; Low grade = $240M ÷ $1200/ton = 200K tons. Volume next year (+20%): High grade = 240K × 1.2 = 288K tons; Low grade = 200K × 1.2 = 240K tons. Savings per ton: High grade = $1500 − $1200 = $300; Low grade = $1200 − $1000 = $200.
math.answer: $134.4M in annual savings by procuring all steel from China (vs. last year's total steel cost of $600M and total costs of $1,525M)

brainstorming.prompt: What are the challenges / risks associated with procuring steel from China?

categories.name: Quality
ideas: Lower or inconsistent quality of Chinese steel may require rework or rejection
Quality standards may differ from local suppliers, risking product defects

categories.name: Supply Chain & Logistics
ideas: Longer lead times to ship steel across the world
Inventory build-up required to buffer longer transit times
Increased transportation costs (though stated costs already include transport and customs)

categories.name: Supplier & Capacity Risk
ideas: Capacity constraints at Chinese steel manufacturers
Concentration risk if a single Chinese supplier is used
Existing relationships with current suppliers who may also supply other raw materials may be disrupted

categories.name: Financial & Currency Risk
ideas: Foreign exchange fluctuations associated with CNY
Hedging costs to manage FX exposure

categories.name: Political & Regulatory Risk
ideas: Many Chinese steel producers are state-owned, introducing geopolitical risk
Potential for tariffs, trade disputes, or export restrictions
Regulatory compliance differences across 200 countries of operation

recommendation: Metal Co's margin problem is primarily driven by rapidly rising raw material costs, especially steel (+$200M over two years), not matched by revenue growth
Procuring steel from China at current prices would save approximately $134M annually — a material reduction against $1,525M total costs — and should be prioritized
risks: Quality and lead-time risks from Chinese suppliers could increase operational disruption
FX and geopolitical risks with Chinese state-owned suppliers
Disruption to existing multi-material supplier relationships
next_steps: Conduct a sourcing RFP with qualified Chinese steel suppliers and validate quality certifications
Quantify FX hedging costs to net them against the $134M gross saving
Analyze remaining cost lines (labour, utilities, outsourcing mix) for additional savings opportunities
Benchmark all cost categories against direct competitors to size the full gap
